tagline: Follow Cow Creek through a canyon shared with rails and gold panning.
intro: Cow Creek Road winds for 45 miles between Riddle and Glendale, following the creek for most of the journey. The paved, two-lane route runs from farms and ranches into deep forest in Cow Creek Canyon. ODOT gives a minimum driving time of one to two hours for its Cow Creek Tour Route; BLM presents the same corridor as a Back Country Byway with railroad and gold-mining interpretation. Old-growth Douglas-fir accompanies the canyon scenery, and portions of the surrounding forest burned in the Douglas Complex Fire in 2013.

The railroad changed Riddle’s business life when it passed between land owned by J. B. Riddle and his brother. Riddle left farming for business and, with his wife Mary Catching, built a hotel in the future town. The canyon’s railroad remains active, while interpretive signs explain the rail line, West Fork and mining. Mining also shaped the corridor’s towns.

From I-5 Exit 103, head through Riddle and west into the canyon. Island Creek Day Use Area offers a creekside picnic or gold-panning stop. Past the West Fork, two steel girder bridges date to 1905. Beyond Skull Creek Campground, the road climbs into pastures and orchards before returning to I-5 at Exit 80 near Glendale.

moments.title: Riddle
moments.text: Nickel mining left visible traces at the start of this drive: mine sites and tailings remain evident at Riddle. The nearby deposits contained the nickel-bearing mineral garnierite, and the mine closed in 1987. The town’s railway identity went through several names: its station was called Riddlesburg by 1881, Riddles in 1882 and Riddle in 1889. The post office kept Riddles until 1910. Cow Creek flows past town before joining the South Umpqua River. Riddle was the site of the last nickel mine and smelter to operate in the lower 48 states.

moments.title: Island Creek Day Use Area
moments.text: Island Creek Day Use Area brings the journey to the creek for picnicking and gold panning. The technique depends on weight: gold is heavier than most stream sediments and gravel, so a pan can collect it with other heavy minerals. Places where the current slows allow gold to settle, including the inside of stream bends and downstream of boulders. Private mining claims are marked along the creek; do not trespass on them. Along the byway, interpretive signs place that activity in the history of local gold mining, the railroad and the former town of West Fork.

moments.title: Glendale
moments.text: Glendale began with a different name and a railroad dispute. After construction of the line south from Roseburg in 1881–83, right-of-way agent Solomon Abraham platted the community as Julia, honoring his wife. Chief engineer A. F. Morris changed it to Glendale after a dispute with Abraham. The post office made that switch between February and August 1883. Fire destroyed much of the business district in 1928, and the town was quickly rebuilt. Glendale is the byway’s connection back to I-5 at Exit 80.

practical: Riddle: Fuel in Riddle; there are no services until the route’s end. Logging trucks are common on blind corners. (checked 2026-10-11)
